L302: We adopt an empirical strategy to construct a near-optimal asymmetric expert placement in two steps: (1) First, we determine the number of replicas for each expert with a greedy algorithm: We maintain a heap of experts sorted by load-per-replica, and iteratively allocate remaining replicas to the expert with the maximum load-per-replica.
L303: (2) Second, we determine the placement of expert replicas across GPUs with Monte Carlo sampling: We randomly generate many placement graphs, and choose the one whose maximum induced subgraph density is minimal.
L304: ### 6.4. Adaptive Replacement
L305: 
L306: Based on the symmetric and asymmetric placements, we further propose an adaptive replacement (AR) mechanism for MicroMoE to optimize performance under dynamic expert loads.
L307: Relationship between token scheduling and adaptive replacement. The adaptive replacement mechanism complements the token scheduling in §cite15†5 by addressing different levels of load balancing. Token scheduling performs transient, fine-grained load balancing through per-micro-batch token arrangement, while adaptive replacement handles long-term, coarse-grained load imbalances through periodic expert arrangement.
L308: Specifically, for moderately imbalanced workloads, token scheduling effectively maintains optimal balance with static, symmetric placements (as shown in §cite28†7.3 ). For highly skewed workloads, MicroMoE adopts asymmetric placements to mitigate coarse-grained imbalances before using token scheduling for fine-grained optimization.
L309: Since asymmetric placements require real-time expert loads, MicroMoE adopts adaptive replacement to monitor expert load distributions and adjust placements when significant distributional shifts are detected.
L310: Implementation of adaptive replacement. We implement the adaptive replacement mechanism in MicroMoE using the placement manager (according to Figure cite101†4 ). (1) During model initialization, the placement manager initializes the model states of all devices using the symmetric placement strategy, providing conservative and general load balancing capabilities. (2) During training, the placement manager monitors expert load information within each micro-batch in the background.
L311: (3) For every few iterations, the placement manager predicts future load distributions using historical data with time series analysis techniques, such as moving averages (cite111†Cong et al., 2024 ). Then, it evaluates the performance of current placements on future distributions using Equation cite109†3 . If the future performance drops below a specific threshold, the placement manager generates new optimal asymmetric placements and re-initializes global model states accordingly.
L312: Difference between MicroMoE’s adaptive replacement and expert scheduling solutions. The system implementation of MicroMoE’s adaptive replacement is similar to existing expert scheduling solutions, such as FlexMoE (cite78†Nie et al., 2023 ) and SmartMoE (cite77†Zhai et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, their design goals and algorithms are fundamentally different:
L313: Design goals: In FlexMoE, changing expert placement is the only means for load balancing. However, in MicroMoE, the primary weapon is token scheduling, while adaptive replacement is a further optimization to token scheduling. Even with static placement, MicroMoE can still achieve good load balancing performance at the micro-batch granularity.
L314: Algorithms: The different design goals of FlexMoE and MicroMoE lead to different placement algorithms. In FlexMoE, all replicas of an expert have identical loads, i.e., the replica load is simply calculated as the expert load divided by the replica count. In contrast, the replica loads in MicroMoE are determined by the LPP cite102†1 . Therefore, MicroMoE requires the graph theory in §cite21†6.1 to guide the placement strategy.
L315: ## 7. Evaluation
L316: ### 7.1. Experimental Setup
L317: 
L318: Testbed. Our testbed consists of 4 nodes, each equipped with 8 NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM GPUs connected via 900 GBps NVLink. Nodes are interconnected using two 400 Gbps Infiniband NICs per node.
L319: Models. We use GPT (cite112†Brown et al., 2020 ) and Mixtral (cite113†Jiang et al., 2024 ) models for evaluation. We use GPT 32$\times$1.3B to represent an MoE model converted from a 1.3B dense GPT model with 32 experts. We pretrain these models with the Wikipedia dataset (cite114†Foundation, 2025 ). A detailed list of model hyperparameters is provided in Appendix cite44†C.1 .
L320: 
L321: Baselines. We compare MicroMoE with four baseline systems.
L322:

L324: Megatron-LM (cite83†Shoeybi et al., 2020 ) is a popular distributed training framework for large language models (LLMs). It supports various parallelism strategies, as well as state-of-the-art optimizations (cite115†Chen et al., 2016 ).

L331: FlexMoE (cite78†Nie et al., 2023 ) achieves load balancing by dynamically adjusting replica counts based on expert loads. FlexMoE places expert replicas across the entire DP group, similar to MicroMoE’s asymmetric placement (§cite23†6.3 ).

L334: DeepSpeed (cite84†Rasley et al., 2020 ) is a high-performance distributed framework for both LLM training and inference. We enable ZeRO-1 (cite88†Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) optimization in DeepSpeed (currently, ZeRO-2 does not support PP, and Tutel (cite105†Hwang et al., 2023 ) does not support top-K>1).
L335: 
L336: We compare two variants of MicroMoE: “MicroMoE (w/o AR)” uses static, symmetric placement (§cite22†6.2 ), while “MicroMoE” uses adaptive, asymmetric placement (§cite23†6.3 -cite24†6.4 ).
L337: Figure 6. End-to-end speedup of different systems compared with Megatron-LM.
L338: Implementation. We implement MicroMoE upon Megatron-LM (cite83†Shoeybi et al., 2020 ). MicroMoE provides a model wrapper similar to Pytorch’s Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) (cite116†Li et al., 2020 ), enabling users to benefit from MicroEP’s fine-grained load balancing capabilities within their training jobs. We modify Megatron-LM, including its MoELayer and DDP with Python, and implement the token scheduling algorithm in MicroEP with C++.
L339: For fair comparison, we also implement SmartMoE and FlexMoE in Megatron-LM, as SmartMoE’s repository is outdated (last commit in 2023) (cite77†Zhai et al., 2023 ), and FlexMoE is not open-sourced (cite78†Nie et al., 2023 ).
L340: Parallelization configurations. Due to the limited inter-node network bandwidth in our testbed, we only employ PP for inter-node parallelism. Specifically, we set the PP degree to the number of nodes used, and the DP degree to 8. We set the EP degree to 4, resulting in 2 EP groups per DP group. We set the parameter $d$ in MicroEP to 2, resulting in a single MicroEP group per DP group. We disable TP due to its high communication overhead.
L341: Other configurations. We use a small auxiliary loss (listed in the appendix) to prevent extreme load imbalance from degrading model accuracy. We enable the distributed optimizers in Megatron-LM, which resembles DeepSpeed’s ZeRO-1 (cite88†Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ). We disable the token dropping mechanism introduced by GShard (cite66†Lepikhin et al., 2020 ). We use BF16 precision.
L342: ### 7.2. End-to-end Performance
L343: Figure cite117†6 shows the end-to-end performance of all systems, varying models and number of GPUs. DeepSpeed exhibits poor performance with 16 or 32 experts. This is because DeepSpeed always adopts a padding mechanism, padding the load of each expert to the maximum expert load (cite66†Lepikhin et al., 2020 ). This mechanism wastes significant time and memory when expert loads are highly imbalanced.
L344: With as few as 8 experts, the inefficiency of padding becomes less significant, allowing DeepSpeed to outperform Megatron-LM due to its system-level optimizations.
L345: Comparing SmartMoE and MicroMoE (w/o AR), where experts have uniform replica counts, MicroMoE (w/o AR) exhibits superior performance, thanks to MicroEP’s fine-grained token scheduling. While SmartMoE attempts to optimize performance by changing expert placement for load balancing among GPUs, it sometimes performs worse than vanilla Megatron-LM. This is because SmartMoE optimizes expert placement based on long-term expert load distributions.
L346: However, expert loads are highly dynamic during training, and SmartMoE’s long-term optimal placement may be sub-optimal for individual micro-batches.
L347: Comparing FlexMoE and MicroMoE (with AR), where experts have varied replica counts, MicroMoE exhibits superior performance, thanks to MicroEP. Compared with Megatron-LM, MicroMoE improves the end-to-end throughput by up to 47.6%, with an average improvement of 36.9%. The average performance improvement of MicroMoE surpasses FlexMoE, the second-best system, by 13.9%.
L348: 
L349: Figure 7. Max GPU load normalized by average GPU load, varying skewness of expert loads. DP_degree=8, num_experts=32.
L350: ### 7.3. Load Balancing Capability
L351: 
L352: We evaluate the load balancing capabilities of SmartMoE, FlexMoE, and MicroMoE with skewed expert loads. We generate expert loads following a Zipfian distribution with skewness $s$, where the probability of a token being assigned to the $i$-th most loaded expert is proportional to $i^{-s}$.
L353: Figure cite118†7 shows the load balancing performance of different systems across varied skewness $s$. SmartMoE’s maximum GPU load increases as load skewness increases. While FlexMoE maintains relatively balanced GPU loads by adjusting expert replica counts, it falls short of achieving optimal load balance due to its lack of fine-grained dynamicity. MicroMoE (random) represents MicroMoE with pure random placement, which performs slightly worse than MicroMoE (w/o AR) with symmetric placement.
L354: MicroMoE (w/o AR) achieves perfect load balance when $s<1$ thanks to MicroEP’s fine-grained token scheduling. Nonetheless, its performance degrades when $s>1$ as uniform replica counts are insufficient for severe imbalances. MicroMoE with asymmetric placements can always achieve perfect load balance, due to the combination of both coarse-grained expert replacement and fine-grained token scheduling.
L355: Overall, MicroMoE exhibits the best load balancing capability among all systems and consistently achieves optimal load balance.
L356: ### 7.4. Execution Time Breakdown
L357: 
L358: Figure 8. Execution time breakdown of an MoE layer. DP_degree=8, num_experts=32, micro_batch_size=8, sequence_length=2048, topK=2, hidden_size=4096, skewness $s$=1.
L359: Figure cite119†8 shows the execution time breakdown of an MoE layer across different systems. We omit DeepSpeed due to its poor performance. For all remaining systems, the primary bottleneck is expert computation time. MicroMoE achieves the shortest computation time by maintaining perfect load balance (with either symmetric or asymmetric placement, as shown in Figure cite118†7 ).
L360: Specifically, the dispatch time consists of two primary components: (1) Preparation time, which includes the all-gather operation of expert load information and the scheduling of MicroEP. While MicroMoE introduces additional overhead in dispatch time due to token scheduling operations, we effectively minimize this impact through overlapping with other operations in Megatron-LM. (2) All-to-all communication time.
L361: Each all-to-all communication in dispatch and combine requires approximately 1.3 ms in Megatron-LM. We further evaluate dispatch time with DeepEP (cite64†DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ), a high-performance all-to-all backend. The results are presented in Appendix cite45†C.2 .
L362: ### 7.5. Overhead Analysis
L363: 
L364: Scheduling Overhead.
L365: 
L366: Figure 9. Scheduling time for MicroEP, varying number of experts and GPUs. Figure 10. Migration time for adaptive replacement of MicroMoE.
L367: We evaluate the scheduling overhead of MicroEP, including the LPP solving time and token routing time. Our evaluation reveals that the LPP solving time is the dominant factor, which scales with the number of experts and GPUs. As shown in Figure cite120†9 , the scheduling overhead remains remarkably low, with a minimum time of approximately 100 us. Even with 64 GPUs and 256 experts, the scheduling time remains under 1 ms.
L368: This minimal overhead per micro-batch enables MicroEP to maintain high training throughput while providing load balancing benefits.
L369: Replacement overhead. The adaptive replacement strategy in MicroMoE necessitates model re-initialization to transition to new configurations. Although replacement is beneficial for load balancing, model re-initialization causes temporary suspension of training. Our evaluation focuses on two key components in the replacement overhead: the migration time of expert parameters and their optimizer states.
L370: As shown in Figure cite121†10 , the total migration time typically spans hundreds of milliseconds across different model configurations. These results emphasize the importance of carefully selecting the expert replacement frequency to optimize the trade-off between per-micro-batch training efficiency and overall replacement overhead.
L371: ### 7.6. Ablation Study
L372: 
L373: Figure 11. Ablation study of dispatch time, with the same setting as Figure cite119†8 .
L374: We conducted an ablation study to evaluate three optimizations in MicroMoE: (1) warm solving in §cite16†5.1 , (2) locality-aware routing in §cite17†5.2 , and (3) overlapping in §cite19†5.4 . All these optimizations aim to reduce the dispatch time. As shown in Figure cite122†11 , both warm solving and overlapping reduce scheduling time, while locality-aware routing reduces all-to-all communication time.
L375: With the combination of optimizations, MicroMoE introduces only 0.4 ms additional dispatch time compared to vanilla Megatron-LM. This modest overhead is substantially outweighed by the reduced computation time, ensuring the overall system efficiency of MicroMoE.
L376: ## 8. Related Work
L377: MoE training systems. Switch Transformer (cite67†Fedus et al., 2022 ) pioneers expert parallelism for transformer-based models. FairSeq (cite123†Ott et al., 2019 ) and FastMoE (cite124†He et al., 2021 ) provide PyTorch (cite125†Paszke et al., 2019 ) plugins to optimize MoE training. DeepSpeed-MoE (cite126†Rajbhandari et al., 2022 ) combines EP with various optimizations, such as ZeRO (cite88†Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) for large-scale MoE training.
L378: Tutel (cite105†Hwang et al., 2023 ) dynamically adapts parallelism strategies and pipeline degrees to handle dynamic workloads of MoE.
L379: MoE load balancing. Many studies propose algorithmic solutions to address the load imbalance issue of MoE. Shazeer et al. (cite56†Shazeer et al., 2017 ) introduce a load-balancing loss, which is further refined by subsequent works (cite67†Fedus et al., 2022 ; cite70†Li et al., 2024 ; cite69†Wang et al., 2024a ; cite127†Wu et al., 2024 ; cite128†Chen et al., 2022 ; cite129†Hazimeh et al., 2021 ).
L380: GShard (cite66†Lepikhin et al., 2020 ) introduces the concept of expert capacity to limit the number of tokens assigned to each expert, which is adopted by later works (cite67†Fedus et al., 2022 ; cite70†Li et al., 2024 ; cite105†Hwang et al., 2023 ). Some studies propose alternative gating algorithms in place of the original top-K gating strategy (cite130†Lewis et al., 2021 ; cite71†Zhou et al., 2022 ; cite131†Roller et al., 2021 ; cite132†Nie et al., 2024 ).
L381: As a systematic approach, MicroMoE is compatible with all these algorithmic solutions.
L382: Many studies offer systematic solutions for load balancing in MoE. FasterMoE (cite65†He et al., 2022 ) models the time consumption of MoE and enables broadcasting the most popular expert to all devices. MoESys (cite133†Yu et al., 2024 ) dynamically adjusts the number of training nodes to ensure load balance in multi-task scenarios. SmartMoE (cite77†Zhai et al., 2023 ) focuses on optimizing expert placement. FlexMoE (cite78†Nie et al., 2023 ) adapts the number of replicas of each expert based on their popularity.
L383: Several other works (cite79†Qing et al., 2025 ; cite81†Skiadopoulos et al., 2025 ; cite80†Wang et al., 2024b ; cite74†Wang et al., 2023 ) embrace similar approaches to FlexMoE, and further reduce the adjustment overhead by integrating expert migration with ZeRO’s communication operations (cite88†Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ). While these solutions typically balance loads at a per-iteration, expert-level granularity, MicroMoE is capable of achieving optimal load balance at a per-micro-batch granularity.
L384: Janus (cite134†Liu et al., 2023 ) proposes a data-centric EP paradigm that avoids the inherent load imbalance issue in conventional expert-centric paradigms. However, Janus requires migrating all expert parameters within every micro-batch, which incurs substantial communication overhead, especially when dealing with large batch numbers and model scales.
L385: ## 9. Discussion
L386: Inference. The load imbalance issue also exists in distributed inference systems with EP (cite84†Rasley et al., 2020 ; cite135†Kwon et al., 2023 ; cite136†Zheng et al., 2025 ). Since inference jobs are more latency-sensitive than training, additional optimizations may be necessary to minimize the scheduling overhead of MicroMoE.
L387: For instance, we can replace the linear programming optimization with randomized algorithms or heuristic algorithms for reduced computational complexity, or predict the expert load distributions ahead of the gate network. We plan to employ MicroMoE for inference scenarios in future work.
L388: Scalability. Scaling MicroMoE to large clusters and increased expert counts introduces new challenges to the system. When scaling up, MicroMoE benefits from an expanded scheduling space, which enhances the load balancing capability of MicroEP. However, this larger scheduling space increases computational overhead in scheduling, potentially degrading the system efficiency.
L389: To compromise between load balancing capability and system efficiency, we can organize GPUs and experts into groups and perform scheduling at the group level, similar to prior works (cite77†Zhai et al., 2023 ; cite66†Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; cite64†DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ).
L390: FSDP. We currently implement MicroMoE based on Megatron-LM’s DDP (cite83†Shoeybi et al., 2020 ). Megatron-LM also supports Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) (cite137†Zhao et al., 2023 ), which resembles DeepSpeed’s ZeRO-3 (cite88†Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ), sharding model parameters and gradients for memory saving. Moreover, FSDP allows users to selectively enable sharding for model modules, providing a fine-grained control of ZeRO’s optimizations. We plan to integrate MicroMoE with FSDP in future work.
L391: ## 10. Conclusion
L392: We propose MicroEP, a novel expert parallelism strategy to achieve fine-grained load balancing in MoE. MicroEP dynamically balances GPU loads within every micro-batch through token scheduling. We primarily make two optimizations in MicroEP: First, we formulate the token scheduling process as a linear programming problem, which can be solved efficiently.
L393: Second, we theoretically analyze the relationship between expert placement and load balancing capacity and develop two placement strategies for different training scenarios. Finally, we propose MicroMoE, an efficient MoE training system based on MicroEP. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that MicroMoE achieves significant performance improvements, with up to 47.6% end-to-end speedup compared to Megatron-LM, and almost consistently maintains optimal load balance across GPUs.
L394: This work does not raise any ethical issues.
